summary: Describes an HTTP API that lets clients interact with a captive portal system, such as the login page at a coffee shop. Clients can discover how to get out of captivity and fetch state about their portal session. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Public Wi-Fi often makes you click through a web page before you can go online. This document gives devices a standard way to ask the Wi-Fi about their session, such as how to get past that page.

subtitle: A small HTTPS and JSON interface that lets a device ask a Wi-Fi network whether it is stuck behind a login page.

tldr.problem: Networks that make users sign in through a web page (a captive portal) give devices no reliable way to learn whether they are captive, or where to go to get out.
tldr.mechanism: The device fetches a JSON document over HTTPS from an API server. The document says whether the client is captive and can point to the user portal, venue information and remaining time or bytes.
tldr.outcome: Clients get authenticated, encrypted access to their captivity state and a standard way to send the user to the portal. It is a Proposed Standard with no replacement listed.

today: RFC 8908 is a Proposed Standard, published in September 2020. The metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFCs. Discovery of the API server is defined separately in RFC 8910.

sections.title: What the Captive Portal API Provides
sections.content:
RFC 8908 defines an HTTP Application Programming Interface that lets a client talk to a captive portal system. It was designed to meet the requirements of the Captive Portal Architecture.

The API provides three things: the state of captivity (whether the client has access to the Internet), the URI of a user-facing web portal that can be used to get out of captivity, and authenticated, encrypted connections using TLS to both the API and the web portal.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a way for your phone to ask the Wi-Fi, 'Am I locked out, and which page do I visit to get in?' The answer comes back over a private, checked connection.

sections.title: Where the API Fits in the Workflow
sections.content:
The Captive Portal Architecture describes three kinds of interaction. Provisioning is where a client learns the network has a captive portal and finds the URI of the API server. API server interaction is where the client asks about its state and gets what it needs to get out of captivity. Enforcement is where a device in the network blocks disallowed traffic.

This RFC defines only the second category. It assumes the client already found the API server during provisioning. Mechanisms for that discovery are defined in RFC 8910.

Two roles are named: the Captive Portal Client, typically an application on the device connected to the captive network, and the Captive Portal API Server, which exposes the API.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting online has three jobs: finding out there is a gate, talking to the gate keeper, and the gate itself blocking you. This document is only about the talking part.

sections.title: Connecting to the API Server
sections.content:
The API server endpoint MUST be accessed over HTTP using an https URI and SHOULD use the default https port. An example URI is https://example.org/captive-portal/api. The client SHOULD NOT assume the URI stays the same for a network, and SHOULD use the discovery or provisioning process each time it joins.

The server must know which client is asking so it can reply with that client's state. If the system identifies clients by IP addresses, the same addresses must be visible to both the API server and the enforcement device. If the server needs identity information it cannot otherwise see, the URI given to the client during provisioning SHOULD be distinct per client, for example https://example.org/captive-portal/api/X54PD39JV.
sections.plainLanguage: Your device always uses the secure web address it was given for this network. Sometimes the address is special to you, like a ticket with your name on it, so the server knows who is asking.

sections.title: Authenticating the Server
sections.content:
Using HTTPS protects the API exchange from other parties on the local network, and lets the client check the server. The client confirms the server has a valid certificate for the hostname provisioned by the network, by checking that a DNS-ID on the certificate equals that hostname.

Revocation checking needs some route to revocation data. OCSP stapling, using the TLS Certificate Status Request extension, SHOULD be used. A captive network SHOULD also permit connections to OCSP responders or Certificate Revocation Lists referenced by the server's certificates, and to NTP servers or other time-sync mechanisms so clients can validate certificates accurately.

Certificates that miss intermediates and rely on the Authority Information Access extension SHOULD NOT be used. If they are, the network MUST allow client access to the host in that URI.

If the client cannot validate the server's certificate, it MUST NOT proceed with any of the API behavior in this document. It then treats the network as if the API were not present.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trusting the answer, your device checks the server's ID card. If the card looks fake or cannot be checked, your device ignores the server completely.

sections.title: The JSON State Structure
sections.content:
Data is written as JSON and carried with the application/captive+json media type. Clients SHOULD include it in an Accept header on GET requests, and servers MUST mark it as the Content-Type of responses.

One key MUST appear at the top level: captive, a boolean saying whether the client is captive. A captive client still gets enough access to do server authentication. Optional keys are user-portal-url (a portal that MUST be accessed over TLS), venue-info-url (a page that SHOULD be accessed over TLS), can-extend-session, seconds-remaining and bytes-remaining.

The server SHOULD include seconds-remaining or bytes-remaining when the client is not captive and the session is limited by time or bytes, and SHOULD omit them otherwise. The byte count is the sum of layer 3 IP packet bytes sent and received, including IP headers.

Clients MUST ignore keys they do not recognize. Servers SHOULD set Cache-Control to private or something more restrictive such as no-store. If a client gets no valid JSON, it SHOULD keep applying the most recent valid content, or act as if the API were absent if it never had any.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer is a short note with a yes or no for 'locked out?' and maybe extras, like the sign-in page, a visitor info page and how much time you have left.

sections.title: An Example Exchange
sections.content:
A client that discovered https://example.org/captive-portal/api/X54PD39JV sends a GET with Accept: application/captive+json. The server answers 200 OK with Cache-Control: private and a body of captive: true and a user-portal-url.

The client sends the user to that portal. Once the user satisfies the requirements, the client SHOULD query the API server again to verify it is no longer captive. The updated response in the RFC has captive: false, the portal and venue URLs, seconds-remaining of 326 and can-extend-session set to true.
sections.plainLanguage: First the answer is 'yes, you are locked out, go to this page.' After you sign in, you ask again and hear 'you are in, and you have 326 seconds left.'

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
One goal is to improve security between clients and captive portal systems. TLS protects client traffic from passive listeners on the local network, and all communication between clients and the API server MUST be encrypted. The API server MUST present a valid certificate on which the client can perform revocation checks.

This validation only confirms the server matches what the network's provisioning mechanism (such as DHCP or IPv6 Router Advertisements) provided. It does not validate those mechanisms or the user's trust in the network.

On privacy, traffic with the user-facing portal may include a full name and credit card details, so both the portal and the API server must be reached only over encrypted connections. The portal hostname comes from the API server, not from the user, so it may contain confusable characters that mislead the user.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is sent in a locked box so nearby people cannot peek. But the lock only proves you reached the address you were given, so you still need to be careful about names that look alike.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the application/captive+json media type, with encoding considerations identical to application/json. IANA also created a registry called Captive Portal API Keys, whose initial contents are the keys in this RFC.

Each entry has a Key, a Type, a Description and a Reference. New entries use the Specification Required policy. The designated expert checks that documentation exists in a permanent, public specification and that new keys have a clear meaning without overlapping existing ones. Keys for non-generic use cases are encouraged to use a domain-specific prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now an official list of the words allowed in the note, so people can add new ones without clashing with old ones.
